questions.prompt: What does a model registry provide?
options: Versioned, approved models with aliases or stages so deployments reference a specific version
questions.explanation: A registry tracks model versions and which is approved for production, so deployments are pinned and rollbacks are possible.

questions.prompt: Which inference pattern suits nightly churn scores?
questions.explanation: Predictions that can be computed ahead of time are batch. Online is request/response; streaming handles continuous events.

questions.prompt: Each prediction response should include the model version that produced it.
questions.explanation: True. Returning (and logging) the version makes regressions attributable and incidents traceable.

questions.prompt: Which rollout sends a small percentage of real traffic to the new version and increases it gradually?
questions.explanation: Canary limits blast radius. Blue-green switches all traffic at once; shadow mirrors traffic without returning the new output.

questions.prompt: The deployment loads `model:latest`. A retrain overwrote it and production quality dropped with no deploy event. What should change?
options: Pin a specific registered version (or a controlled alias) and keep previous versions for rollback
questions.explanation: Loading 'latest' lets deployments change silently, and overwriting removes the rollback path. Both are listed mistakes.

questions.prompt: Which belong in a model quality gate before promotion? Select all that apply.
options: Score on a fixed test set vs the current champion
questions.explanation: Gating only on code tests is a listed mistake; model quality needs its own gates.

questions.prompt: Offline accuracy is 0.91 but production accuracy is 0.74. Training code computes `age_years = days / 365.25`; the serving code uses `days / 365` and fills missing values with 0 instead of the training median. What is this and the fix?
options: Training-serving skew; package preprocessing with the model artefact (e.g. one pipeline) and add a skew test that runs the same raw record through both paths
questions.explanation: Preprocessing implemented twice diverges. Bundling it with the model and testing that both paths produce identical features prevents skew.

questions.prompt: Leadership wants to know whether a new recommendation model increases revenue. Which rollout gives that evidence?
options: An A/B test splitting users with statistical analysis
questions.explanation: Shadow cannot measure user impact because its output is never shown. A/B tests measure business outcomes.

questions.prompt: A colleague cannot reproduce last quarter's model. Which records would have made it reproducible?
options: Code commit, data version, hyperparameters, random seed, pinned dependency versions and metrics, recorded in experiment tracking
questions.explanation: Notebook-only training without seeds, data versions or pinned dependencies is a listed mistake.

coding.title: Training-serving skew test
coding.prompt: Write `skew_report(records, train_fn, serve_fn, tol=1e-9)` where both functions turn a raw record dict into a features dict. Return a sorted list of `"<record index>:<feature>"` strings for every feature whose values differ (numbers compared with absolute tolerance `tol`, other values with `==`) or which is missing from one side.
coding.explanation: Running identical raw records through both code paths and diffing the features is the skew test from the lesson. It catches subtle differences such as 365 vs 365.25 or different imputation long before they show up as lower production accuracy.
hints: Compare the union of feature keys from both outputs.
Use a tolerance for numbers and `==` for everything else.

tests.name: Missing feature
tests.code:
assert skew_report([{}],lambda r:{'x':1,'y':2},lambda r:{'x':1})==['0:y']
assert skew_report([{}],lambda r:{'x':1.0},lambda r:{'x':1})==[]

coding.title: Champion-challenger promotion gate
coding.prompt: Write `can_promote(challenger, champion, min_gain, max_slice_drop)` where both arguments are dicts with `"overall"` (a score) and `"slices"` (slice name -> score). Return `(ok, reasons)`. Add `"overall gain too small"` if `challenger overall - champion overall < min_gain`; add `"slice drop: <name>"` (sorted by name) for each slice where the challenger is more than `max_slice_drop` below the champion; add `"missing slice: <name>"` for champion slices absent from the challenger. `ok` is True when there are no reasons. Use a tolerance of 1e-9 in comparisons.
coding.explanation: Promotion should compare against the current production model, not an absolute number, and must look at slices so an overall gain cannot hide a regression for one group. Missing slices are treated as failures because 'not measured' is not 'fine'.
hints: Loop over the champion's slices in sorted order.

tests.name: Promotes a clear improvement
tests.code:
ok,r=can_promote({'overall':0.9,'slices':{'a':0.9,'b':0.88}},{'overall':0.85,'slices':{'a':0.86,'b':0.88}},0.01,0.01)
assert ok is True and r==[], r

tests.name: Blocks hidden slice regressions
tests.code:
ok,r=can_promote({'overall':0.92,'slices':{'a':0.99}},{'overall':0.85,'slices':{'a':0.9,'b':0.8,'c':0.7}},0.01,0.02)
assert ok is False and r==['missing slice: b','missing slice: c'], r
ok,r=can_promote({'overall':0.851,'slices':{'en':0.9,'fr':0.6}},{'overall':0.85,'slices':{'en':0.88,'fr':0.7}},0.01,0.02)
assert r==['overall gain too small','slice drop: fr'], r
